title: Candy Corn Bag

drivers.name: Price increase (6.0%)
drivers.evidence: Two recent weeks at $4.08 saw sales of 13 and 3 units (vs baseline 10.2). Sales dropped 70% and 71% vs baseline. This aligns with the 6% price hike and past sensitivity. Noise-adjusted effect of price increases is consistent with ~35% reduction.

adjustment.analysis: The baseline median is 10.2. A 6.0% price increase to $4.08 (from $3.85) is a known demand-lowering driver. Past promotions show median uplift of x2.15 vs baseline, but noise-adjusted is only x1.45. The 2026-09-07 Labor Day promotion (10% off) lifted sales to x1.75, but this week has no promotion—only a price increase. Price hikes reduce demand; the 2026-09-28 and 2026-10-05 weeks at $4.08 saw low sales (13 and 3 units), suggesting price sensitivity. No event or promotion is scheduled. The classical model suggests no uplift, but the price increase is a valid downward driver. Evidence is strong enough to adjust, but not extreme. Noise-adjusted effect of price increase is modest but consistent.

brief:
PRODUCT: Candy Corn Bag | category Candy | Store #12 (Austin, TX)
TARGET WEEK: 2026-11-09 to 2026-11-15 (5 weeks after the last week with sales data)

KNOWN PLAN FOR THE TARGET WEEK:
  events: none
  shelf price: 4.08 (+6.0% vs regular price 3.85)

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 10.2 | 5%-95%: 0.0 - 24.9 | 10%-90%: 0.0 - 19.4

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-85% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
